title: Members of Georgia’s Election Board Have Been Coordinating With Cleta Mitchell’s Network
author: Doug Bock Clark
content:
In the run-up to the midterms, members of Georgia’s State Election Board and
much of its professional staff were coordinating with an activist group led by
Cleta Mitchell, the conservative attorney who worked with President Donald
Trump [to try to overturn his
defeat](https://www.propublica.org/article/cleta-mitchell-elections-trump) in
the 2020 election.

The [board sets the swing state’s election rules](https://seb.ga.gov/about-
us/), oversees the conduct of its election officials and investigates
allegations of fraud.

Recordings of private calls and events reviewed by ProPublica show current and
former state board members working with the Election Integrity Network and
allied organizations on shared priorities. Among them: [advancing the
use](https://x.com/Election_Adv/status/2090441612690087975?a=jSGjVn8IWaQMzlNBcyM&s=20)
of a controversial, error-prone software tool known as ELLY to search voter
rolls for purportedly suspicious voters.

The state board’s current vice chair, Janelle King, and her predecessor,
Janice Johnston, have both attended meetings of EIN or VoterGA, an aligned
organization whose membership and goals significantly overlap with EIN.
Johnston [retired in June](https://www.ajc.com/politics/2026/06/one-of-trumps-
pit-bulls-resigns-from-state-election-board/) but still plays an active role
in state election matters behind the scenes.

At an [August 2025 fundraiser for
VoterGA](https://rumble.com/v6x9l18-a-lakevew-evening-with-garland-favorito-
and-cleta-mitchell-
august-5-2025.html?e9s=src_v1_s%2Csrc_v1_s_o%2Csrc_v1_rso&sci=e41dcc04-050a-4e78-91b9-4b82e323ca74),
Mitchell declared she loved Johnston and King, who were both present. “You
know, we’ve worked so hard together,” Mitchell said.

![A woman wearing a suit jacket sits beside a woman wearing a brown shirt,
behind a curved wooden table with laptops, microphones, and nameplates as King
speaks during a board meeting, filmed by cameras in the
foreground.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/20261112-ga-election-Janice_King.jpg?w=1149)Janice
Johnston and Janelle King at a March meeting of the State Election Board.
Johnston resigned from the board in June. Mauricio Rodriguez Pons/ProPublica

At least three members of the state board’s eight-person professional staff
have participated in EIN meetings, including people who handle allegations of
voter fraud and misconduct by election officials.

The board’s executive director, James Mills, likewise has worked closely with
members of the EIN, according to five sources with knowledge of these
interactions, board documents and EIN communications shared with ProPublica.  

EIN’s close ties to the board and its staff have given it extraordinary
influence over how elections are run in Georgia, experts said. In particular,
the group has been able to enlist the board’s help in getting counties to
remove voters from their rolls based on information from ELLY.

“Trump allies captured the State Election Board to keep claims of a stolen
2020 election going and tilt Georgia elections toward Republicans,” said Max
Flugrath, a director at Fair Fight Action, a voting advocacy nonprofit that
has closely tracked the board’s and the network’s actions. “EIN was the
behind-the-scenes driver spearheading these changes.”

The board’s chair, John Fervier, told ProPublica he had not known about EIN’s
sway over the board or its staff, but said he’d long sensed that an outside
force was shaping the board’s actions.

“The more I look into this, the more I’m realizing that the Election Integrity
Network has been having an undue influence on the State Election Board, and
that needs to cease,” he said in an interview, though he declined to go into
specifics about personnel matters. “I’m looking forward to changes in how the
election board operates.”

![A man in a suit jacket sits behind a curved wooden
table.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/20261112-ga-
election-Fervier_2.jpg?w=1149)John Fervier has chaired the Georgia State
Election Board since 2024. Mauricio Rodriguez Pons/ProPublica

Fervier has [called a special meeting for
Friday](https://mailchi.mp/seb/special-called-meeting-
september-3-4763704?e=a40e7e69ef), in part to discuss [personnel
matters](https://mcusercontent.com/ef3e6521f1c5021bdec8b070f/files/d45772aa-e5cb-e517-caee-4d158fa72672/Agenda_Special_Called_Meeting__November_13_2026.pdf).

In response, Garland Favorito, an EIN leader and head of VoterGA, [called on
social media for his
followers](https://x.com/VoterGa/status/2120531176393748973?ref_src=twsrc%5Egoogle%7Ctwcamp%5Eserp%7Ctwgr%5Etweet)
to inundate state board members with messages defending Mills and other
staffers associated with the group.

“There is a significant possibility that these members will vote to terminate
the Executive Director, investigators or possibly even staff members, any of
which would destroy the SEB as we now know it,” Favorito wrote on Wednesday,
referring to the State Election Board. “As most of you know, the SEB staff has
made remarkable historical progress this year in … accountability for election
corruption and much more. The Executive Director and staff deserve raises for
amazing performances, not threats of termination.”

In interviews in late September, Johnston did not directly answer questions
about her relationship to EIN. “I’m all about election integrity, wherever it
comes from,” she said. She acknowledged she had remained involved with board
affairs after her retirement. “It gets in your blood,” she said. Two days
later, she [posted on social
media](https://x.com/Election_Adv/status/2105261527137759626?a=1QozBuoSImlSuk2t6d0&s=20)
that “Cleta Mitchell, Election Integrity expert has the right ideas” about how
elections should be run.

Johnston did not answer detailed questions about her relationship with EIN and
affiliated groups.

![A woman wearing a brown turtleneck speaks into a gooseneck microphone while
gesturing with her hands behind a wooden table during a
meeting.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/20261112-ga-
election-Janelle_King_1.jpg?w=1149)King was appointed to the board by the
Republican-led Georgia House in 2024. Mauricio Rodriguez Pons/ProPublica

King acknowledged she spoke about election matters with activists from EIN and
VoterGA, but said they did not influence her decisions. She also said she saw
no problem with EIN activists working for the board, though the staff is
supposed to be independent and nonpartisan.

“As long as they are representing the SEB well, fine,” she said in an
interview. “If they choose to become members of an organization in their
private time, that is their choice.”

When a reporter recounted instances in which staffers had worked to advance
EIN goals in their official capacity, she said she was unaware of this. “That
is the first I’ve heard about it,” she responded.

Mills declined to answer questions from ProPublica about his relationship to
EIN.  

Mitchell did not respond directly to ProPublica but, after receiving detailed
questions, put [a post on X celebrating EIN’s
work](https://x.com/CletaMitchell/status/2120918850027790749?a=0ABVSF8VSBKb7NFkxB8&s=20)
with the election board. “An election integrity group is working with election
officials to oversee elections,” she wrote. “Wow! What a discovery!!! Pulitzer
anyone?”

Favorito called the idea that the board and its staff had been working
secretly with the EIN and VoterGA a “patently false conspiracy theory.”

EIN has been deeply entwined with conservatives’ efforts to reshape Georgia
elections since at least 2024.

That year, ProPublica’s reporting revealed, [EIN members secretly pushed a
rule](https://www.propublica.org/article/georgia-election-board-vote-
certification) through the State Election Board allowing local officials to
potentially delay certifying the state’s vote count. A [court subsequently
struck down](https://www.propublica.org/article/georgia-election-results-
certification-counting-votes) the change, which [experts had warned could
enable county election boards to disrupt certifying the election if Trump had
lost](https://www.propublica.org/article/georgia-election-rule-could-exclude-
votes).

In late 2025, the board played a role in instigating the Trump
administration’s [unprecedented effort to reinvestigate alleged 2020 voting
irregularities](https://www.propublica.org/article/fbi-fulton-county-voting-
records-search-warrant), formally [asking the Justice
Department](https://sos.ga.gov/sites/default/files/2025-09/seb_july_29-30_2025_seb_meeting_summary_of_minutes.pdf)
to [obtain Fulton County election records](https://courthousenews.com/doj-
sues-fulton-county-for-ballots-from-2020-election-other-states-for-voter-
rolls/) subsequently seized by the FBI. It was a move pushed by the EIN. The
[affidavit authorizing the
raid](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28887701-full-and-unredacted-
fulton-warrant-with-names-govuscourtsgand3554521072/#document/p1) cited
Johnston and King as witnesses. The affidavit also cited a report [put
together by an EIN researcher](https://www.propublica.org/article/kevin-
moncla-election-researcher-fulton-county-georgia) compiling activists’
debunked allegations of fraud.

In recent months, EIN’s allies and participants at the state board pushed
counties to use ELLY, a tool developed by an EIN member, to search voter rolls
for signs of fraud and purge suspect registrants.

ELLY aggregates public data from state voter files, federal change-of-address
records, tax documents, obituaries, property websites like Zillow and other
sources, but doesn’t have access to personal identifiers such as Social
Security numbers or full dates of birth. As a result, voting rights groups
have said, ELLY often erroneously flags legitimate voters.

Nonetheless, before the midterms, the State Election Board’s investigative
staff pressured Chatham County, a Democratic stronghold, to purge more than
200 registered voters that the tool identified as questionable, the [Atlanta
Journal-Constitution reported](https://www.propublica.org/article/election-
challenge-forsyth-county-georgia).  

After the election, a Forsyth County election board member who is also a
member of EIN submitted ELLY data questioning the validity of over 60 ballots,
including four cast by people who were supposedly dead. [ProPublica
found](https://www.propublica.org/article/election-challenge-forsyth-county-
georgia) that all four were, in fact, alive. The board rejected the
challenges.

[EIN
members](https://x.com/Election_Adv/status/2090441612690087975?a=6lpQDeZdlijmZzUPKjk&s=20)
and state board officials have [defended ELLY’s
accuracy](https://seb.ga.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Minutes-
August-19-2026.pdf).  

The EIN’s connections to the board carry additional importance in light of
last week’s election results, in which Democrats wrested control of all
statewide offices and the state House from Republicans. The House [appoints a
member to the State Election
Board](https://codes.findlaw.com/ga/title-21-elections/ga-code-sect-21-2-30/),
opening the door to change.

Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms ran on a platform that promised a new approach
to the election board.

“The State Election Board has become mired in political games, conspiracy
theories, and partisan interference,” the [platform
stated](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1cturSXcz2qK8yvtxRCyVwqUD47T39ibQ/view).
Bottoms’ platform pledged that she would “work with the General Assembly to
eliminate the current State Election Board and replace it with a stronger,
more independent election oversight structure that is insulated from partisan
manipulation.”

Fervier is part of the board’s four-member Republican majority, but he has
clashed repeatedly with Johnston, King and Mills and has effectively been
relegated to a member of the minority at times.

![Two men wearing suit jackets sit beside a woman wearing a green shirt at a
curved wooden table with monitors, microphones, and nameplates during a board
meeting. ](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/20261112-ga-
election-Mills_Fervier_King.jpg?w=1149)State Election Board Executive Director
James Mills, Fervier and King at a board meeting in Fayette County in August
Mauricio Rodriguez Pons/ProPublica

Emails and communications between board members and staff obtained by
ProPublica via public records requests show that Fervier and other board
members who oppose steps supported by the EIN have been excluded from some
board hiring decisions.

Earlier this year, Fervier [publicly accused
Mills](https://www.ajc.com/politics/2026/07/georgia-election-board-promotes-
new-voter-roll-tool-ahead-of-midterms/) of going beyond what the board had
authorized in calling for the Justice Department and the Department of
Homeland Security to intervene to assess the security of the state’s voting
machines.

“Activists should not control the board,” he told ProPublica. “I’m really
looking forward to this meeting because I think that we’re going to address
some issues that should have been addressed awhile ago.”

The post [Members of Georgia’s Election Board Have Been Coordinating With
Cleta Mitchell’s Network](https://www.propublica.org/article/georgia-election-
board-cleta-mitchell-midterms) appeared first on
[ProPublica](https://www.propublica.org).
